title: Self Closing Tags
summary:
Introduces void (self-closing) elements, focusing on the horizontal rule
and line break
: how their single-tag syntax differs from a closing tag, when to use each, and why br must not replace p. The exercise formats a William Blake profile page with h1, p, br and hr, and the solution adds a diff-checking tip for finding bugs.

concepts.heading: Void vs non-void elements
points: Non-void elements (h1-h6, p, ...) have an opening tag, content in between, and a closing tag.
A void element is one that is not allowed to contain any content. Because there's nothing to wrap, it is written as a single tag: no separate opening and closing tags.

The name of the element goes first, then a space (by convention), then a forward slash, then the closing angle bracket:
and
.
(Extra) Other void elements met later in the course include , , and .

concepts.heading: Where the slash goes (and which slash)
points:
In a closing tag such as

, the slash comes right after the opening angle bracket, before the tag name.

In a void element such as
, the slash comes after the tag name, just before the final angle bracket. Easy to mix up, so check the position.
It must be a forward slash (/, leaning right), never a backslash (\, leaning left).

concepts.heading: <hr />: horizontal rule
points: Renders a horizontal line across the page at the point where it appears in the document.
Use it to divide content and signal that what follows is a separate, unrelated part, e.g. placing it between two paragraphs puts a line between them.
(Extra) Semantically, hr marks a thematic break in content; its look (thin grey inset line by default) can be restyled with CSS.

concepts.heading: : line break
points: Forces the following text onto a new line without starting a new paragraph.
Meant for text that is still one paragraph but whose line divisions carry meaning: poems (line breaks control rhythm, rhyme and where to pause) and postal addresses.

Example used: the opening four lines of Blake's 'Auguries of Innocence'. Written inside a single p without br they run together into one line; with a br at the end of each line they display as proper verse.
The br itself holds no content; it only marks where the break goes.

concepts.heading: Do's and don'ts
points: Don't use br to fake new paragraphs (stacking breaks to push text down). It harms accessibility: screen-reader users rely on real p elements to understand and navigate content.
Create a new p for every real paragraph; reserve br for line breaks inside one paragraph (poem, address).

Both
and
(and
and
) are valid HTML. In HTML5 the trailing slash is ignored: the parser already knows br and hr are void after reading the tag name.

Recommended style in the course: keep the trailing slash, because it makes void elements easy to spot when reading code and avoids hunting for a closing tag that doesn't exist. Expect to see the slash-less form online too.

concepts.heading: Debugging tip: diff your code against the solution
points: Copy solution.html into one side of diffchecker.com and your index.html into the other, then click 'Find Difference'. Every mismatch gets highlighted.
Harmless differences also show up, e.g. an extra space between 'Blake' and changes nothing in the rendered page.

Real bugs stand out: if the closing tag is mistyped (e.g. the h is dropped so it reads </1>), the h1 never closes and everything after it renders as giant heading text. The diff points straight at the broken tag.

task.name: 2.3 Void Elements: William Blake profile
task.starting_point: Download and extract the lesson's starter folder and open index.html. It contains plain, unformatted text: the name William Blake, his London address on four lines (17 south molton street / London / W1K 5QT / UK), and two Wikipedia paragraphs about him. In the preview it is one jumbled block.
task.goal: Format the page with everything learned so far (h1, p, br, hr) so the preview matches goal.png.
steps: Wrap 'William Blake' in an h1: it's the most important text on the page.
Wrap the four address lines together in one p (an address is a single paragraph).

Add
at the end of each address line so each part sits on its own line within that paragraph. Typing it once and copy-pasting to the other lines is fine.
Wrap the first Wikipedia block in its own p, and the second block in another p, so the biography shows as two separate paragraphs.
Insert <hr /> between the address paragraph and the first biography paragraph, separating the name/address from the description.
Preview and compare with goal.png, then compare with solution.html. Optionally paste both into diffchecker.com to spot any differences.
task.expected_result: Large 'William Blake' heading; the address on four stacked lines with no gaps between them; a grey horizontal line; then two separate biography paragraphs with a gap between them.

pitfalls: Writing the slash in the closing-tag position (</br>) or using a backslash (<br \>).
Trying to put content inside a void element, or adding a closing tag such as </hr>.
Using several br elements to create space between paragraphs instead of separate p elements (bad for screen readers).
Splitting the address into four separate p elements: it is one paragraph broken into lines.
A typo in a closing tag (e.g. </1>) leaves an element open and restyles everything after it; diff against the solution to find it quickly.

(Extra) The reference repo's files include a personal 'Made with ... by Harshit Soni' footer that is not part of the course; leave it out. Its index.html is already completed, so it doesn't show the unformatted starter.
